JSON: Name: ss_kspace_mtl_segmentation Title: Self-supervised k-space pretraining with multi-task learning for robust cardiac MRI segmentation under respiratory motion artifacts Short Hypothesis: Pretraining an encoder via self-supervised reconstruction of k-space simulated respiratory motion artifacts and subsequently training a multi-task network that jointly predicts image quality labels and myocardial segmentation will increase segmentation robustness (higher DSC and lower HD95) and reduce clinical biomarker error (LVEDV, LVEF) on motion-degraded cardiac MRI compared with equivalent models trained without the proposed pretraining or without the joint IQA task. Related Work: Existing methods for cardiac MR segmentation under motion primarily follow supervised encoder-decoder pipelines (2D/3D nnU-Net variants) with heavy use of data augmentation and ensembling. Image-quality-assessment (IQA) approaches typically use slice-wise or volume-wise CNNs or transformer classifiers often pretrained on ImageNet; they show reasonable detection of gross artifact but poor fine-grained severity classification. Some prior work simulates motion in image space or k-space to augment training, and a few methods apply self-supervised pretraining or multi-task setups, but these remain siloed. Limitations include (1) reliance on natural-image pretraining that does not model MR physics, (2) augmentation schemes that do not match realistic k-space artifact statistics, (3) sparse use of joint IQA+segmentation training and limited evaluation of downstream biomarker accuracy, (4) heavy dependence on ensembles and large backbones that reduce clinical feasibility, and (5) lack of systematic ablation quantifying contributions of k-space pretraining, multi-task learning, and pseudo-labeling. Abstract: Respiratory motion degrades cardiac MRI (CMR) image quality and undermines automated segmentation and downstream clinical measurements. We propose a pipeline combining self-supervised k-space pretraining with a multi-task segmentation and image-quality-assessment (IQA) network to improve robustness to respiratory motion artifacts. First, an encoder is pretrained to reconstruct artifact-free images from synthetically corrupted k-space inputs that emulate respiratory motion statistics. Second, the pretrained encoder initializes a segmentation network trained jointly to predict myocardial/LV/RV masks and a three-level IQA label. The main contribution is integrating MR-physics-aware self-supervision with a task-coupled training objective to align representations with both reconstruction and clinical downstream tasks. We will evaluate the approach on a controlled motion-degraded CMR dataset and external multicenter cohorts, measuring segmentation overlap, boundary accuracy, and errors in clinically relevant biomarkers. Expected outcome: improved segmentation robustness and more accurate clinical biomarkers on motion-degraded scans relative to supervised baselines and ablated variants, without large inference-time ensembles. Experiments: Datasets: primary: CMRxMotion dataset (320 volumes from 40 volunteers; subject-level split: 20 train, 5 val, 15 test). External: M&Ms-1 and M&Ms-2 and ACDC for cross-dataset generalization (held-out centers/patients, pathologies). Preprocessing: convert DICOM to NIfTI, resample to 2.0x2.0 mm in-plane, slice thickness 8 mm; z-score normalize per volume. Proposed pipeline components: (A) self-supervised k-space pretraining: train encoder to map corrupted k-space reconstructions to artifact-free images using L1+SSIM loss; (B) multi-task finetuning: encoder + decoder segmentation head (predict LV, MYO, RV masks) and IQA classification head (3 classes: mild/intermediate/severe). Baselines: 1) supervised 2D nnU-Net trained from scratch; 2) nnU-Net with ImageNet-pretrained encoder; 3) nnU-Net pretrained via image-space autoencoder; 4) top-challenge ensemble proxy (replicate UA-SVCC or Med-Air architecture if available); 5) multi-task model without k-space pretraining. Ablation studies: (i) remove k-space pretraining, (ii) replace k-space with image-space pretraining, (iii) single-task segmentation vs multi-task IQA+segmentation, (iv) disable pseudo-labeling (if used) vs enable, (v) ensemble vs single model. Training details: 2D slice-wise training, batch size 48, AdamW, initial LR 1e-4 with cosine decay, up to 400 epochs with early stopping on validation DSC. Use 5-fold subject-level cross-validation on training set for hyperparameter selection. Evaluation metrics: segmentation: Dice per structure, HD95 (mm); IQA: Cohen's weighted Kappa, per-class precision/recall; clinical biomarkers: LVEDV, LVESV, LVEF, RVEDV, LVM — report MAE, RMSE, MAPE compared to ground truth; compute: inference time per volume and peak GPU VRAM. Statistical analysis: bootstrap 10,000 samples for 95% CIs; Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired comparisons, Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple tests; significance threshold p<0.05. Reporting: report per-IQA-stratum performance (IQA labels 1/2/3), external dataset generalization, and ablation effect sizes. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Simulation mismatch: synthetically corrupted k-space may not capture full variability of patient motion, leading to limited transfer to real-world clinical artifacts. 2) Label noise and IQA ambiguity: subjective IQA labels may introduce noise, biasing multi-task training and harming segmentation. 3) Data diversity: training primarily on healthy volunteer scans may not generalize to pathological anatomies, limiting clinical applicability. 4) Pseudo-label propagation risk: if pseudo-labels are used for unlabeled external data, errors may reinforce model biases. 5) Computational cost: k-space pretraining and multi-task networks may increase training compute and memory requirements; large models could impede deployment. 6) Overfitting to augmentation: heavy augmentation strategies risk models learning augmentation artifacts instead of robust anatomical features. 7) Evaluation bias: using the same center/scanner for training and testing may overestimate performance; cross-center variability may reveal lower gains. 8) Clinical biomarker sensitivity: small segmentation improvements might not translate to clinically meaningful reductions in biomarker error for some patient subgroups.
